note: Source triangulation for /how-to-clean-grout. Each source accessed via WebFetch or WebSearch on 2026-04-20. Quoted snippets are direct lifts from the source page (short-quotation editorial use).

sources.name: Bob Vila
keyClaims: 8-step escalation order: water + nylon brush -> vinegar + water (sealed only) -> baking soda + vinegar -> hydrogen peroxide -> oxygen bleach -> commercial cleaner -> steam -> chlorine bleach (last resort)
Vinegar only on SEALED grout; unsealed cement-based grout can be damaged by acids
Steel-wool and hard steel brushes damage tile + strip sealant
Chlorine bleach erodes grout with long-term use
quotedSnippets: If you've tried any or all of the above methods before you apply chlorine bleach, be sure to rinse the surface completely before proceeding with any chlorine bleach products. This is especially true of vinegar, because traces of vinegar mixed with bleach will emit a toxic gas into the air.
Baking soda alone works for unsealed surfaces
Vinegar should only be used on sealed grout

sources.name: This Old House
keyClaims: Escalation: mildest solution first -> commercial cleaners -> professional contractor
Do NOT use chlorine bleach on grout: discolors grout over time and causes deterioration
Acid-based cleaners unsafe for marble and limestone
Wait 24 hours after cleaning before applying sealer
Steam loosens dirt before chemical treatment but requires ventilation
quotedSnippets: Grout is a porous substance, and grout-filled joints can easily collect dirt.
Always begin with the mildest solution when you first start cleaning grout.
You should not use bleach to clean grout...it discolors grout over time.
Sealing grout is necessary for deep cleaning but not quite as important for lighter cleaning.
Clean your grout regularly and seal it after deep cleaning for sparkling tiles.

sources.name: Family Handyman
keyClaims: Escalation: water + stiff brush -> 50/50 water + vinegar -> baking soda paste -> hydrogen peroxide -> heavy-duty bleach (last)
Metal-bristled brushes strip sealant, damage grout, scratch tile
Toxic-chemical handling requires ventilation
quotedSnippets: Avoid brushes with metal bristles since those could strip away any sealant, damage the grout and scratch the tile.
If plain water no longer keeps your grout clean, then it's time to add vinegar.
If you've tried all these solutions and still find yourself with unsightly grout, it's time to move to the next level.
Be sure that you handle any toxic chemicals with care and ventilate your workspace the best you can.

sources.name: Tile Council of North America (TCNA)
sources.note: TCNA is the trade body for US tile manufacturers + installers. Primary-source authority on tile/grout chemistry. NOT currently in data/trusted-sources.json tier_primary list; belongs there. Flagged for trusted-sources addition.
keyClaims: Cement-based grout should be cleaned with ALKALINE cleaners (Spic and Span, Mr. Clean), NOT acidic
Acid cleaners dissolve cement in grout; grout manufacturers do NOT recommend acids; regrouting may be needed
Do NOT use oil or wax-based cleaners (Murphy's Oil Soap, Pine-Sol): residue builds in porous grout
Enzyme-based cleaners (laundry pre-soak type) are effective
Cementitious grout SHOULD be sealed; epoxy grout is virtually stain-proof without additional sealing
quotedSnippets: it is better to clean grout with an alkaline cleaner (Spic and Span, Mr. Clean, etc.) than an acid based cleaner.
do not clean with oil or wax based cleaners (Murphy's Oil soap, Pine Sol, etc.).
it is not recommended by the grout manufacturers – needing to regrout is sometimes the result.

sources.name: Consumer Reports
keyClaims: CR tested 7 grout cleaners at home, following label instructions
Tested: performance + ease of use + odor + abrasiveness
Two tested products carry EPA Safer Choice labels
Full product rankings gated behind membership; summary-level signal accessible
quotedSnippets: We tried all the cleaners on the grout in our homes, following the instructions on the labels
A few months ago, I tried a grout cleaner I randomly plucked off the shelf at Home Depot, and it did next to nothing.

Consumer tip sheet is general guidance; industry standards behind paywall

contradictions.positions: Bob Vila: allowed on SEALED grout only. TCNA: avoid acids — they dissolve cement. This Old House: acid-based unsafe for marble/limestone. Family Handyman: 50/50 water+vinegar listed as step 2.
contradictions.editorialResolution: Page will recommend AVOIDING routine vinegar use on grout. TCNA is the primary-source authority (industry trade body) and its guidance against acids outweighs the editorial tier-2 baseline. Vinegar moves to a 'what NOT to use' callout rather than a promoted step. Aligns with Safe Surface Desk warranty-first posture.

contradictions.positions: Bob Vila: last-resort-only. This Old House: DO NOT USE (erodes grout). Family Handyman: heavy-duty option with ventilation caveat.
contradictions.editorialResolution: Chlorine bleach moves to 'what NOT to use' callout, with a narrow exception: visible mold that survives oxygen bleach. TOH's direct prohibition combined with the grout-erosion mechanism justifies demoting it below oxygen bleach.

contradictions.positions: TCNA: alkaline (explicit). CR + Bob Vila: mostly silent on pH. Stone-safe cleaners (Miracle Sealants): pH-neutral for natural stone.
contradictions.editorialResolution: Page angle: ALKALINE for cement grout, pH-NEUTRAL for natural-stone tile. Two-axis decision: grout chemistry vs surrounding-tile chemistry. This is the differentiator most how-to guides miss.
